content:
## Top Attractions in Jelsa

Jelsa sits on the north coast of Hvar island, about 27 km east of Hvar Town and 15 km from Stari Grad. It is a compact town of stone houses, pine-covered headlands and a long, flat waterfront. Most main sights are within a 10-minute walk of the harbour, which makes it easy to cover on foot.

### Pjaca Square and the Seafront Promenade

Pjaca, the main square, is the centre of Jelsa. It opens onto the harbour and is lined with cafés, ice-cream counters and restaurants. A coffee costs roughly €2–3, and a scoop of ice cream about €1.50–2.50.

The promenade runs from Pjaca along the water in both directions. The best time to walk it is early evening, when the stone facades turn warm and the fishing boats settle in. It is free and open at all hours.

The harbour has been renovated and has 54 moorings for yachts, sailboats and catamarans, with water, electricity, showers and toilets. Even if you do not sail, a walk along the quay shows Jelsa's role as a working port.

### Fortress Church of St. Mary of Mercy

The fortress church of St. Mary of Mercy (Sv. Marija od Milosrđa) is Jelsa's most recognisable historic building. It dates from the 16th century, with earlier roots, and was fortified against Ottoman raids. It stands a short walk from Pjaca. Opening times are irregular and mostly tied to services, so the exterior and the setting are the main draw. Allow 15–20 minutes.

### Churches of St. John and St. Fabian and Sebastian

The parish church of St. Fabian and Sebastian and the small Church of St. John are in the older streets behind the waterfront. The Church of St. John, from the 17th century, is easy to miss, so look for it among the narrow lanes. Dress modestly if you want to enter.

### Jelsa Park (Perivoj)

The pine and palm park by the harbour offers shade in summer and is free. It suits families and is a good place to wait for an evening ferry or bus.

## Best Beaches in Jelsa

Jelsa's beaches are mostly pebble and concrete bathing platforms, shaded by pines. They do not compare to Brač's sand spit, but the water is clear and calm.

- **Mina Beach:** The town beach, within easy walking distance of the centre. It has shallow water and suits children.
- **Grebišće and Lučica:** Small pebble bays on the headlands beside the town. Pines give shade and the sea is clear. Sunbeds are limited, so bring a towel and arrive early in July and August.
- **Dubovica Beach:** A quiet pebble cove on the coast beyond the town. It is the top-rated beach in the area, and many visitors rank it as the best swim near Jelsa. Parking is limited, so go before 10:00 or after 16:00 in summer.

Most beaches have cafés nearby, but facilities are basic. Take water and snacks to the remoter coves.

**Opinion:** Dubovica looks perfect in photos, but in July and August the access road and parking fill up by late morning. Swimming at Mina or Lučica, a short walk from town, is far less stressful and almost as pleasant.

## Water Sports and Active Things to Do

### Windsurfing and Sailing

The channel between Hvar and Brač has reliable afternoon wind in summer, and Jelsa has a windsurf centre (Bota Windsurf Center) that rents equipment and gives lessons. Beginners should book a morning lesson, when the wind is lighter. Kayaks and stand-up paddleboards can usually be rented along the beach front for roughly €8–15 per hour.

### Adventure Park Hvar Jelsa

The Adventure Park offers paintball, battle archery, human table football, giant boxing, bubble football and axe throwing. Paintball needs groups of four or more, and bookings are private, so no strangers join your game. It suits stag and hen groups and families with teenagers. Book ahead in peak season.

### Cycling

The roads around Jelsa, through lavender fields, vineyards and pine woods, are suitable for road and e-bikes. Rental shops in town offer e-bikes for a half or full day. Avoid the midday heat from late June to August, and start before 9:00.

## Wine, Food and Local Flavours

Jelsa sits in one of Hvar's main wine areas. Local producers make red plavac mali and white bogdanuša and prč. Winery tastings in the Jelsa area generally run from about €15–25 per person with snacks such as cheese, olives and prosciutto. Tomić Winery and Dubokovic Wine are among the best-rated stops. Book ahead, since many are family-run and visits are by appointment.

On the waterfront, konobas serve grilled fish, black risotto and gregada, a Hvar fish stew. A main course costs about €14–25, and a fish platter for two usually costs €60 or more. Fish is sold by weight, so ask the price per kilo before ordering.

A farm visit is a good alternative for families. Family Farm Kod Kučera has donkeys and goats, goat cheese tastings and views across to Brač and the Makarska coast.

## Best Time to Visit Jelsa

- **May–June:** Warm weather, quieter streets, sea around 19–22°C.
- **July–August:** Peak season, with the warmest water (about 24–26°C) and the most crowds, mainly in the evenings.
- **September:** Warm sea, thinner crowds and grape harvest. This is the best month for most visitors.
- **October–April:** Many cafés and restaurants close or reduce hours, and ferries are less frequent.

Jelsa is calmer and cheaper than Hvar Town. A couple in shoulder season can expect around €150–200 per day all-in, including meals out and a rental car for a few days, with peak-season Hvar Town costing 40–60% more.

## Getting Around Jelsa

The centre is flat and walkable. Jelsa has a catamaran connection with Split, with one useful departure per day each way and a fare of roughly €10 one way in peak season. Car ferries run to Stari Grad, about 15 minutes by road from Jelsa, and cost around €40 per car from Split. Cazmatrans buses connect Jelsa with Hvar Town, Stari Grad and Vrboska for roughly €3–5 per trip. Check the seasonal timetable, as it is limited outside summer.

Taxi transfers are fixed-price on the island. From Jelsa, expect about €28 to Stari Grad, €20 to Vrboska and €55 to Hvar Town.

## Practical Tips for Visiting Jelsa

- **Parking:** Spaces near the harbour fill up by 10:00 in summer. Park at the edge of town and walk.
- **Sun and heat:** The strongest sun hits between 12:00 and 16:00. Plan beach time for early morning and late afternoon.
- **Cash:** Small cafés, church entrances and some beach kiosks still prefer cash. Carry small euro notes.
- **Footwear:** Bring water shoes for pebble beaches and rocky entries.
- **Evenings:** The promenade is liveliest after 20:00. Jelsa is a relaxed town and does not have Hvar Town's club scene.

## Where to Stay

Most visitors choose private apartments and small hotels within a 5-minute walk of Pjaca. Pine-covered headlands to the east and west have quieter rooms near the beaches. Book early for July and August.

faq.question: What is the number one thing to do in Jelsa?
faq.answer: Walking the seafront promenade and spending an evening on Pjaca square is the core Jelsa experience, followed by swimming at the pine-shaded beaches. Dubovica Beach is the top-rated beach in the area.

faq.question: Is Jelsa worth visiting?
faq.answer: Yes, for a quieter and cheaper alternative to Hvar Town. It has a historic centre, clear water, wine and good conditions for windsurfing. It is less suited to travellers who want nightlife.

faq.question: How many days do you need in Jelsa?
faq.answer: Two to three days is enough to see the town, swim at the main beaches and do one activity such as windsurfing or a winery tasting. Add more days if you plan to use Jelsa as a base for exploring the island.

faq.question: Does Jelsa have good beaches?
faq.answer: Jelsa has several pebble beaches with clear water and pine shade, including Mina, Grebišće and Lučica. They are free and close to the centre. Dubovica, a short drive away, is the most popular cove.

faq.question: How do you get to Jelsa from Split?
faq.answer: A catamaran runs from Split to Jelsa once daily in each direction, takes about 1 hour and costs around €10 one way in peak season. Alternatively, take a car ferry to Stari Grad and drive about 15 minutes. A private boat from Split takes around 55 to 60 minutes and starts at about €370 per boat.

faq.question: Is Jelsa good for families?
faq.answer: Yes. The shallow town beach, the shaded park, the adventure park and farm visits with donkeys and goats suit children of most ages. The flat centre is also easy with pushchairs.

faq.question: Is Jelsa cheaper than Hvar Town?
faq.answer: Yes. Accommodation, food and drinks cost noticeably less in Jelsa than in Hvar Town, especially in July and August. A taxi between the two costs about €55, so a day trip is affordable.

quickAnswer: The best things to do in Jelsa are walking the seafront promenade and Pjaca square, visiting the 16th-century fortress church of St. Mary of Mercy, swimming at Mina, Grebišće and Lučica beaches, windsurfing, tasting Hvar wine at local wineries, and trying paintball at the Adventure Park. Dubovica Beach is the best-known swim nearby.
